Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 3 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Narrative and Fiction Portfolio Revision

Lesson Focus

Lesson 3: Narrative and Fiction Portfolio Revision

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.REV.01 — Revision from feedback.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.NAR.01 — Narrative development and structure; MLA.CW.NAR.02 — Point of view, pacing, and detail; MLA.CW.FIC.06 — Fiction craft and character development.

What You Will Learn

  • Diagnose story problems beneath reader symptoms.
  • Revise character desire, conflict, causality, point of view, and pacing as an integrated system.
  • Use feedback without flattening voice or intentional ambiguity.
  • Document narrative revision as evidence of growth.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 3 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
narrative arcThe shaped progression of conflict, choices, consequences, and change.The arc moves from concealment to discovery to a costly decision.
causalityThe relationship in which one event or choice meaningfully produces another.Because Mara hides the letter, her friend makes the wrong choice.
character motivationThe desire, fear, belief, or need that explains a character’s actions.Fear of repeating her father’s mistake motivates Lena to leave.
sceneA dramatized unit of action occurring in a particular time and place.The confrontation unfolds moment by moment in the kitchen.
summaryCompressed narration that covers time or information without dramatizing every moment.One paragraph summarizes the quiet months between conflicts.
narrative distanceHow close the narration feels to a character’s immediate thoughts and perceptions.Sensory detail and fragments reduce the distance during the panic.
focalizationThe perspective through which narrative information is perceived or filtered.The scene is focalized through a child who misreads the adults.
turning pointA choice, discovery, or event that changes the direction or stakes of a narrative.Finding the second key forces the narrator to reconsider the accusation.
earned endingA conclusion prepared by earlier choices and patterns while still allowing surprise.The ending surprises readers but resolves the repeated promise motif.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which sequence has the strongest causality?

A. A storm begins. Later, the character remembers a song. Then a key appears.

The events are adjacent, but no clear choice or consequence connects them.

B. The character hides the warning, so the crew leaves; the resulting accident forces her to confess.

Correct. Each choice produces a consequence that changes the next event and the character’s situation.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 3 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Diagnose and Revise the Narrative System

Step 1 — Translate Feedback into a Diagnosis

Reader symptomPossible causeQuestion
“I lost interest.”Unclear desire, repetitive obstacle, delayed consequenceWhere did attention fall, and what changed there?
“The ending came from nowhere.”Missing setup or causal linkWhich earlier choice should prepare this result?
“I do not know who is speaking.”Uncontrolled focalization or weak cuesWhose knowledge and language govern the scene?

Step 2 — Map Desire to Consequence

For every major scene, complete: Character wants ___, but ___, so the character chooses ___, causing ___. “And then” signals chronology; “therefore” or “but” signals causality.

Pause and Choose: Strengthen Narrative Causality

Which scene plan creates a causal chain rather than a list of events?

A. “Mara misses the bus, and then it rains, and then she finds a key, and then she enters the house.”
Weaker choice. Events occur in sequence, but the plan does not show how desire, obstacle, and choice produce consequences.
B. “Mara needs shelter before the storm, but the station closes, so she uses the key she promised not to touch, causing the locked house to become her only option.”
Stronger choice. Desire meets an obstacle, the character chooses under pressure, and that choice creates the next problem. The plot develops through causality.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 3 — Control Point of View

  • Choose what the focal character can perceive and know.
  • Match diction and comparisons to that consciousness.
  • Signal intentional shifts through scene breaks, headings, or unmistakable voice.
  • Remove convenient knowledge inserted only to solve the plot.

Step 4 — Revise Pacing by Importance

Use scene for consequential choices and discoveries. Use summary for routine travel, repeated attempts, or lower-impact time. Expand the moment readers must interpret; compress what they only need to know.

Pause and Choose: Earn the Ending

A protagonist suddenly solves the central conflict with an ability never mentioned earlier. What is the strongest revision?

A. Replace the convenient solution with a choice shaped by earlier desire and consequences, or plant the ability and its cost well before the ending.
Stronger choice. This makes the outcome retrospectively logical and keeps character action central. Preparation supports surprise without announcing it.
B. Keep the sudden ability and add an explanation after the conflict is solved.
Weaker choice. A late explanation does not create prior causality. The solution still arrives from outside the narrative system rather than from established choices and consequences.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 5 — Earn the Ending

  1. List the ending’s decisive action or realization.
  2. Trace which earlier desires, images, promises, and choices prepare it.
  3. Add preparation without announcing the answer.
  4. Remove coincidences or late devices that replace character choice.
  5. Test whether the ending is both surprising and retrospectively logical.

Revision Order

Motivation → causality → scene order → point of view → pacing → sentence craft → conventions. Do not polish a scene that the structural revision may remove.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 3 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Narrative Revisions

Example 1 — Repairing Motivation and Causality

Draft: Lio suddenly enters a burning archive to recover a stranger’s notebook.

  1. Symptom: the action feels unbelievable.
  2. Diagnosis: no established desire connects Lio to the risk.
  3. Revision: earlier, Lio learns the notebook contains testimony that could clear his mother’s name.
  4. Causal chain: desire for truth → fire blocks access → choice to enter → injury and recovered evidence.
  5. Result: the same action becomes character-driven rather than arbitrary.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which revision most directly repairs Lio’s unbelievable decision to enter the burning archive?

A. Add more flames and smoke so the scene feels dangerous enough to justify his action.
Weaker response. Increasing danger raises the stakes but does not supply the missing motivation connecting Lio to the choice.
B. Establish earlier that the notebook contains testimony that could clear his mother’s name, creating a desire strong enough to explain the risk.
Stronger response. This revision repairs causality by linking a prior desire to the obstacle, decision, consequence, and recovered evidence.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Controlling Point of View

Draft: “Mara wondered whether Theo lied. Across town, Theo hid the letter and regretted everything.”

  1. Problem: the scene begins in Mara’s consciousness and enters Theo’s without a signal.
  2. Option A: remain with Mara and infer Theo’s lie through behavior.
  3. Option B: insert a scene break and establish Theo as the new focal character.
  4. Decision depends on purpose: uncertainty favors A; dramatic irony may favor B.

Example 3 — Expanding the Right Moment

Draft: “After months of searching, Nia found the missing ledger. She read the final name and decided not to publish it.”

  1. Diagnosis: two consequential moments are compressed.
  2. Revision: summarize months of routine searching, then dramatize the discovery.
  3. Slow time with sensory detail, selected entries, and Nia’s physical response.
  4. Give the decision an immediate cost or consequence.
  5. Result: pacing teaches the reader what matters.

Transfer Test

For each revision, state: symptom → diagnosis → structural change → textual evidence → reader effect.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: A character suddenly lies to protect a stranger. Add one earlier detail that makes the action character-driven without explaining everything.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: Earlier, the character notices the stranger wearing the same emergency-service badge once carried by a missing sibling. That evidence creates a personal reason to protect the stranger while leaving room for uncertainty.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 3 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Narrative and Fiction Portfolio Revision

Purpose

Revise narrative and fiction at the structural, scene, and sentence levels while preserving the work’s central purpose.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Support decisions with precise evidence from your portfolio work.

Source for Your Work

Revision problem: A story has a compelling ending, but the protagonist’s decisive action depends on information introduced only in the final paragraph.

1. Plan Before You Work

Portfolio DecisionEvidence and Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each precisely.
Strongest current evidenceName the piece, passage, or feature.
Most important improvementDescribe the needed change and intended effect.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger author decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Add a sentence near the beginning that directly announces the ending so readers are prepared.
B. Plant meaningful evidence earlier, develop the character’s motivation through scenes, and preserve discovery while making the ending earned.

3. Apply the Lesson

Select one narrative or fiction piece of at least 500 words. Complete a three-level revision plan—development, organization, and language—then produce a revised version with at least one consequential change at each level.

4. Revise with Purpose

Present three before-and-after excerpts and explain how each revision improves coherence, characterization, pacing, or impact.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to specific portfolio evidence.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on the audience.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves quality, coherence, or readiness.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Narrative and Fiction Portfolio Revision

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Revision Crossroads

In the first draft, a character decides to leave home after one short argument. The setting is vivid, but the decision feels unearned. Peer feedback asks for more history; the writer worries that added explanation will slow the pace.

A global revision changes structure, development, motivation, pacing, or meaning. A local revision improves sentences, diction, clarity, or conventions.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. What global problem prevents the turning point from feeling earned? Propose two ways to address it without adding a long explanation.
  2. Which existing strength should the writer preserve while revising, and how can it support the new development?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which revision plan improves motivation while protecting pacing?

A. Add a paragraph that explains the entire family history immediately before the argument.
B. Plant two earlier details or actions that reveal the history gradually, then let the argument activate those established pressures.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Complete a substantial revision of one 700–1,000 word narrative or fiction piece.

  1. Diagnose: State the intended effect and identify the highest-impact global problem.
  2. Plan: Map the opening, development, turning point, and resolution; note what must move, expand, cut, or transform.
  3. Revise: Strengthen character motivation, conflict, pacing, point of view, and thematic consequence.
  4. Edit: Improve paragraphing, sentence control, diction, dialogue, and conventions.
  5. Reflection: Provide two before-and-after excerpts and explain how the revisions improve the whole piece.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Perform a reverse outline of the revised piece. Change one scene or paragraph whose function is unclear, then explain the structural improvement.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
